extracted.intended_audience: Congressional staff, policymakers, EPA officials, state regulators, and legal/enforcement professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Transcribed congressional hearing discussing EPA investigation, testing, enforcement, remedies, and consumer/state impacts related to vehicle 'defeat devices' that circumvent emissions standards. The page records questions of Members and testimony about authority, testing protocols, mitigation, recalls, and interagency/state coordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defeat device definition / identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Software that circumvents EPA emissions standards (a dual-calibration strategy allowing vehicles to operate one way during testing and differently on the road).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA issued a Notice of Violation alleging VW/Audi diesel cars included such software; EPA and California were notified by VW; EPA does not need to 'unpack 100 million lines of code'—real-world testing that activates the device and tailpipe measurements are the key to detection.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA authority & limits under the Clean Air Act (individual prosecutions)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA representatives stated they would not anticipate the EPA 'going after individuals' and that they were not aware of any Clean Air Act provision authorizing prosecution of individuals for the types of acts discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While individual criminal liability is discussed as a possibility, EPA testimony indicates Clean Air Act enforcement typically targets manufacturers/companies; criminal or individual liability would involve separate investigative/coordinated processes (e.g., DOJ).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacturer responsibility for repairs and recalls
rubrics_metrics.description: Liability for excess emissions and the responsibility to repair/fix noncompliant vehicles lies with the manufacturer (Volkswagen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA will order recalls when it is confident the remedy is effective; until a recall is ordered, EPA provides consumer guidance (e.g., cars are safe to drive). The company is responsible for repairs; consumers are not to be held responsible for fixing manufacturer-installed defeat devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigation obligation to 'make the environment whole'
rubrics_metrics.description: Settlements and enforcement seek mitigation to address environmental harm (i.e., forward-looking actions to improve air quality beyond minimum legal requirements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigation can take many forms (example: funding third-party programs such as cleaner wood-stove changeouts) because pollution already emitted cannot be removed; mitigation plans are a standard component of consent decrees and settlements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing regime: unpredictability and real-world monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must use unpredictable testing and a combination of laboratory cycles plus on-road/real-world monitoring to detect defeat devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA changed its testing to be less predictable; future approach will combine the five prescribed lab cycles, off-cycle dyno testing, activity testing (downloading software/data), and mobile real-world emissions measurement to activate and detect defeat strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that manufacturers test and submit data for new models
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturers are required to test every new model of vehicle and submit that data to EPA for review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA audits a percentage of submissions by lab testing and reviews design data; EPA also conducts independent audits and real-world checks to verify manufacturer-submitted results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for manufacturer cooperation and document production
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA and enforcement partners require internal investigation results and documents from the manufacturer to understand how defeat devices worked and who was responsible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA (and DOJ/state AGs) issue official document requests; VW had not agreed to share internal investigation results at the time and EPA will inform the committee if documents are not provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer impacts as a central factor in remedy choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection of a remedy must consider effects on vehicle owners and consumers; consumer interests are central to EPA's review of options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA seeks remedies that will work for consumers and the environment, and explicitly recognizes owners as 'innocent'—remedies and recall procedures should minimize undue burden on owners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculation of excess emissions and mitigation planning
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must calculate the excess tons of pollution caused by noncompliant vehicles and use that calculation to determine appropriate mitigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA acknowledged it had not yet done the math to quantify excess emissions (e.g., vehicles emitting 10–40 times allowed amounts) and will determine mitigation measures based on those calculations during the investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential for civil/criminal enforcement in coordination with DOJ
rubrics_metrics.description: Enforcement actions may include civil penalties and coordination with the Department of Justice for other remedies; ongoing investigations will determine specifics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's enforcement office has taken initial action and is working with DOJ; witnesses cautioned against speculating about final courses of action while investigations continue, but criminal action against a corporation or individuals is treated as a possible outcome to be determined by the investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of penalty funds toward mitigation projects
rubrics_metrics.description: Fines or penalties assessed may be used to fund mitigation projects that improve air quality in affected communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example provided: penalty funds used to implement third-party wood-stove changeout programs to reduce local pollution; mitigation can be implemented through consent decrees and settlements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource needs for robust, expanded testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective detection of deceitful software requires resources for expanded real-world testing capabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ICCT recommended providing EPA more resources to perform real-world testing rather than relying on happenstance NGO discoveries; EPA affirmed it has capabilities and will augment testing partnerships (e.g., California, Environment Canada).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and reporting to Congress and states
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA committed to keep the committee informed of testing progress, procedures, data, and to provide state-level breakdowns and other relevant information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee requested information on state antitampering laws, fines, criminal penalties, vehicle registration locations, and a breakdown by state of affected vehicles to support oversight and public-health attribution analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies must be effective and validated before ordering recalls
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA will not order a recall until it is confident that the proposed remedy will effectively make the vehicles compliant and work for consumers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA expects to review proposed remedies from Volkswagen and evaluate impacts (including trunk space or other mechanical consequences for Gen 1 cars) before ordering recalls; effectiveness and consumer impacts are central criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritization of testing scope (diesel first)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA prioritized testing beginning with all light-duty diesel vehicles to evaluate the use of defeat devices across the fleet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testing of the first batch of vehicles was underway at the time, with cooperation from California and Environment Canada; EPA started with diesels but will consider broader testing if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: State law role in consumer fines and inspections
rubrics_metrics.description: State laws govern enforcement like emissions inspection fines; EPA's federal enforcement does not automatically equate to state-level fines for owners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA noted that fines are a matter of state law; once EPA-approved remedies fix vehicles so they pass state inspections, owners should not be subject to state fines or inspection failures related to the defeat devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Owners considered innocent; protection from repair liability
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA asserts vehicle owners are not at fault for manufacturer-installed defeat devices and should not bear responsibility for repairs required to make vehicles compliant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA guidance to consumers emphasized that vehicles are safe to drive and that repair obligations rest with the manufacturer, not the owner, pending recall and remedy procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple enforcement partners (state AGs, DOJ, EPA collaboration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Enforcement and investigation involve coordination among EPA, state attorneys general, and the Department of Justice to determine remedies, penalties, and possible criminal or civil actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA staff met with state air directors and noted ongoing contact from state attorneys general; cooperation is expected to help determine where vehicles are registered and how to mitigate excess pollution at state/local levels.
